newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Peters sees RBNZ action if super vote passed.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Peters sees RBNZ action if super vote passed.

text.p: New Zealand Deputy Prime Minister and Treasurer Winston Peters said on Wednesday the Reserve Bank of New Zealand would have to make a "countervailing response" if a proposal for a compulsory superannuation scheme was approved by voters in September.
He said this was because the scheme would withdraw money from the economy and therefore slow growth.
Peters told reporters in Sydney after a luncheon address to the Trans-Tasman business circle that the Reserve Bank had not included the effects of a compulsory savings scheme in its forecasts.

"I'd expect a countervailing response to there being somewhat less money in the economy as a result of the savings strategy," Peters told reporters when asked if the Reserve Bank should ease policy if the vote is successful to compensate for lower consumption and higher savings.
He said some commentators had forecast a compulsory superannuation scheme would trigger a growth slowdown as savings increased and consumption fell, but he personally did not agree with that.
Peters released a white paper on Monday outlining the structure of a compulsory superannuation scheme that would be put to a referendum in September.

The plan requires all earners to contribute three percent of their income to the scheme to build up a lump sum of about NZ$120,000 that would used to buy an annuity after retirement equal to the current state pension.
The compulsory superannuation scheme, to be implemented in July next year if passed in the referendum, was a key part of the election campaign of Peters' party, New Zealand First.
NZ First is the junior partner in a coalition with the conservative National Party.
A recent poll of showed opposition to the scheme rising to 63 percent from 59 percent in May.

Peters told his audience of Australian business people that the New Zealand government could not afford to continue with its current state-funded superannuation system because of an impending surge in the numbers of elderly people and the lower
Opponents of the compulsory scheme had argued the current superannuation system was sustainable as long as debt rose, taxes rose or government spending fell, Peters said.
Any of these options were clearly unsustainable, he said.
